1. Deep learning with connection sparsity (i.e., pruning) is statistically equivalent to a single-layer network with a reduced number of parameters.

(i) deep networks can be sparsified without loss of prediction accuracy and that (ii) the sparsity-inducing regularizers we study are not only effective in practice, but also statistically well justified.

(a) the prediction accuracy of neural networks can be controlled by a combination of the number of nodes and the number of connections, (b) sparse neural networks with a large number of nodes are more accurate than dense networks with a small number of nodes, (c) the number of nodes can be reduced to a fraction of the number of data samples, (d) the number of connections can be reduced to the number of data points, (e) the prediction error is controlled by the network width

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we establish a connection between deep learning and classical results in statistics, such as the VC theory and the theory of empirical risk minimization.
we provide a mathematical foundation for deep learning with sparse connectivity and node activations.
we provide statistical prediction guarantees for connection- and node-sparse deep learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the performance of neural networks is governed by the underlying graph of the network and that sparsity-inducing regularizers are key ingredients to achieve optimal statistical performance.
the prediction accuracies for neural networks with sparsity-inducing regularizers can be controlled by the sparsity of the networks and the complexity of the underlying function.
the performance of deep learning with sparsity-inducing regularizations is not necessarily better than that of standard ridge regularization.
